text.title: Nvidia relief rally fades as Nasdaq falls 1.5%; defensives and Dow rise, Anthropic slips below IPO price
text.summary: The Nasdaq fell 1.5% and the S&P 500 lost 0.5% to 7,201.09 as Monday's Nvidia-fueled rally unwound. The Dow rose 0.9% and the Russell 2000 gained 0.6%, so the damage was concentrated in technology, which fell 3.3%. Money moved into health care, staples and real estate. The 10-year yield slipped 2 bp to 4.90% and the dollar index fell 0.5%. Oil rose 1.8% to $81.63 on Middle East shipping risk, while gold dropped 2.7% and Bitcoin lost 2.3%. The common thread is investors questioning how much AI-related risk is already priced in, even as Dell reported strong AI demand.
text.rates: The 10-year yield fell 2 bp to 4.90% and the 2-year was unchanged at 4.63%. Both remain well below levels of a week ago, down 20 bp and 17 bp respectively. WSJ described Treasuries as mixed ahead of Wednesday's PCE inflation and GDP data. Bloomberg reported bond traders hedging the risk that Fed hikes and the stock slide slow the economy. Lower yields eased pressure on long-duration stocks but did not offset the tech selloff. The dollar index fell 0.5% to 103.82. Gold dropped 2.7% despite the softer dollar, and the headlines do not explain that move.
text.breadth: Only technology (-3.3%) and industrials (-0.5%) fell among the sectors. Health care, staples, real estate, energy, financials, communication services, discretionary and materials all rose. Large-cap growth took the hit while the Dow and small caps rose, a defensive tilt within equities. The VIX eased 1.0% to 26.36, but it is still 43.3% higher than a month ago.
text.context: The S&P 500 is down 1.9% over five days and 6.2% over a month, 7.0% below its one-month high. The Nasdaq is 10.6% below its high. J.P. Morgan's weekly recap notes that large-cap growth is down 13.6% year to date as of Nov 20, while large-cap value is up 18.9%, and energy leads sector returns. Per the recap, the S&P 500 traded at 16.4x forward earnings as of Nov 20, though MarketWatch argues stocks are still not cheap.
text.takeaway: Sharp swings around a few heavily weighted AI names show how concentrated index returns can be. Diversification across sectors, styles and asset classes is designed for periods when leadership rotates quickly like this.
text.talk: Stocks gave back part of Monday's Nvidia-driven bounce, with technology weak while health care, staples and the Dow held up. Investors are now watching Wednesday's inflation and growth data and any tariff announcements.

drivers.h: Huang relief rally runs out of steam
drivers.t: Monday's surge came on Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO. Tuesday, traders weighed what the reinstatement does not fix, including regulatory issues and an investigation into his relationship with a former Megaspeed executive. Republicans in Washington are also worried about national security, so political risk remains. Because Nvidia is such a heavy index weight, its reversal pulled the Nasdaq down 1.5% and the technology sector down 3.3%. The S&P 500 gave back 0.5%.

drivers.h: AI debt worries and Anthropic's slide
drivers.t: CNBC reported that fears about some companies' AI-related debt rose a day after Huang's return. Separately, Anthropic closed below its $83 IPO price less than a week after listing. It opened at $111.50 on Nov. 19 and has fallen steadily since, on track to lose nearly $200 billion in value. When newly listed AI names trade poorly and funding costs for AI projects come into question, investors tend to demand more evidence of returns on heavy spending. That weighs on the richest valuations first. Analysts remain largely positive on Anthropic, per CNBC.
drivers.impact: AI funding worries weigh on growth

drivers.h: Dell strong, but AI read-through mixed
drivers.t: Dell reported sales that more than doubled on AI server demand, a record $132 billion backlog and a $25 billion buyback. The stock rose 2.5% after hours. The read-across is uneven, though. HPE sank despite its strongest growth ever and a raised forecast, which suggests strong results are already expected. A BNP Paribas analyst also warned of a mounting memory-chip oversupply risk, which pressured Micron. Investors are separating AI demand from AI pricing power and valuation.
drivers.impact: Dell up after hours; HPE, Micron down

drivers.t: Health care rose 3.0%, helped by Insmed's 14% jump after Sanofi agreed to buy it in pharma's biggest deal in three years. Staples gained 1.7% and real estate 1.3%. The Dow's 0.9% gain, versus the Nasdaq's decline, shows rotation out of crowded growth names rather than a broad exit from equities. Bloomberg also noted that quant funds are struggling to keep pace with how quickly the market narrative is shifting.
drivers.impact: Health care, staples up; tech down

drivers.h: Oil firms on Middle East shipping risk
drivers.t: WTI settled up 1.8% at $81.63 after recovering from early losses. Continuing attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz are keeping a risk premium in prices and limiting the downside from expectations of a global supply surplus. Houthis also hit Riyadh's tallest tower. Energy was up 1.0% on the day. Oil is still down 19.8% over one month, so today's rise is a bounce within a larger decline.

earnings.t: The record $132 billion backlog and raised AI server outlook, plus a $25 billion buyback, added to the beat. The stock rose after hours, in contrast with HPE's reaction to its own strong results.
